newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese investors positive on HK, down on Bangkok.
newsitem.headline: Japanese investors positive on HK, down on Bangkok.

text.p: Japanese investment trust funds remain positive about the future of Hong Kong stocks despite their seemingly overheated bull-run ahead of the territory's handover to China.
By contrast, fund managers were divided whether the worst was over for the ailing Thai stock market.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index ended the last trading day under British colonial rule on Friday at a record closing high of 15,196.79. Hong Kong markets are closed from Monday through Wednesday this week to mark the handover.
Slower economic growth in the Asian region and a financial crisis in Thailand had prompted Japanese investors to shun Asia over the past year in favour of U.S. and European stocks.

Japanese investment trust management firms held a total of 382 billion yen ($3.32 billion) worth of stocks in Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines as of the end of April, down 32 percent from the end of September 1996, according to data from Japan's Investment Trusts Association.
But within those countries, fund managers said they are overweight in Hong Kong and have no immediate plans to cut that weighting.

"Hong Kong's price-earnings ratio is currently around 17. Historically, we have seen it go higher, so the Hong Kong market is not necessarily overheated," said a fund manager of Global Equities at Daiwa Asset Management Co. Ltd.
"There seems to be room for China's interest rates to come down this year. Such factors are positive for Hong Kong," he added.
Japanese investment trusts held 183.6 billion yen ($1.59 billion) worth of Hong Kong stocks at the end of April, down 28 percent from the end of September 1996.
But because they cut back even further in the other Asian markets, Hong Kong's weighting among the five Asian markets increased to 48 percent in April from 45.5 percent at the end of September 1996.

"Money is flowing into Hong Kong from mainland China at a fast pace and Hong Kong's property market remains buoyant. We plan to maintain a high weighting in Hong Kong," said Susumu Fujikawa, portfolio manager at Nikko Securities Investment Trust and Management Co. Ltd.
Unless there is a clear setback in Hong Kong's booming property market, his company does not plan to cut its weighting for Hong Kong, he added.
Fund managers said they are underweight in Thai stocks. They are also divided about the Thai market's prospects.
Japanese investment trusts held 56.8 billion yen ($493 million) worth of Thai stocks at the end of April, down 45 percent from the end of September 1996.
Thai stocks accounted for 14.9 percent of stocks held by investment trust funds in the five Asian markets, down from 18.4 percent in September 1996.

"The Thai market has lost more than two-thirds of its value from its all-time high. We could say the market has hit rock bottom. All the negatives about the Thai economy seem to be priced in," said the fund manager at Daiwa.
"However, we are in no hurry to buy. We are carefully looking for the best time to buy in the next few months," he said.

Thailand's SET index fell to a low for the year of 457.97 points after the resignation of Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on June 19. It has since recouped some of its losses after the government issued decrees last Tuesday aimed at averting a crisis in the finance and property sectors.
The SET index ended at 527.28 on Monday. Its all-time high is 1,789.16 set in January 1994.
Nikko's Fujikawa was more pessimistic about Thailand.
"Our weighting in Thailand is currently zero. We see no reason to change that in the near future. Not until the country is forced to devalue its currency," Fujikawa said.

He added a devaluation of the baht would result in downward revisions in But a devaluation would be positive in the long run as it would help Thai exports regain competitiveness, he said. ($1=115 yen)
